stimuli.text: A block of mass 3 kg on a 20° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 8 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.15. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 0.3 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.19\cos(9t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A hoop (I = MR²) and a solid cylinder (I = ½MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 0.6 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal ledge 5.5 m high at 15 m/s. How far from the base of the ledge does it land?

options.why: Correct. Fall time from the height, times the horizontal speed.
Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.
Fall time is √(2h/g).
Take the square root for the time.

questions.stem: A 7 kg cart moving at 3 m/s collides with and sticks to a 2 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.
Kinetic energy is not conserved here.
Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.
The carts share the momentum.

questions.explanation: v_f = 7·3/9 = 2.33 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 7 J.

questions.stem: Two springs with constants 90 N/m and 70 N/m are connected in series and support a 2.5 kg mass at rest. How far do they stretch in total?

options.why: Series and parallel rules are reversed.
Both springs share the load.
The force is the weight, mg.
Correct. k_eq = k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂).

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 2.1 m swings about a pivot at one end with small amplitude. What is its period?

options.why: d is L/2, the distance to the center of mass.
I = mL²/3.
Correct. T = 2π√(I/(mgd)) with I = mL²/3 and d = L/2.
A rod is a physical pendulum, not a simple one.

questions.stem: A 0.8 kg ball hits a wall at 16 m/s and rebounds at 13 m/s. The contact lasts 0.06 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.
Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.
Include the rebound.
Divide by time.

questions.stem: A 63 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating upward at 4 m/s². What does the scale read?

options.why: Correct. The scale reads the normal force: N − mg = ma (up positive).
Include gravity.
The acceleration changes the normal force.
Check the direction of the acceleration.

questions.stem: A curve of radius 70 m is banked so that a car at 27 m/s needs no friction. What is the banking angle?

options.why: Measure the angle from the horizontal.
Use tan θ = v²/(rg), from dividing the force components.
Square the speed.
Correct. tan θ = v²/(rg).

questions.stem: A cart moving at 6 m/s accelerates uniformly at 6 m/s² over 34 m. What is its final speed?

options.why: The equation has 2aΔx.
Take the square root.
Square roots do not add term by term.
Correct. Use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 260 kg load 17 m at constant speed in 16 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: That is the work; divide by time.
Include g.
P = W/t.
Correct. P = mgh/t.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 6x^3$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 2$$ m to $$x = 5$$ m?

options.why: Divide by n + 1 when integrating.
Correct. W = ∫F dx.
Integrate; do not just evaluate F.
The force is not constant.

questions.stem: A planet has 10 times Earth's mass and 3 times Earth's radius. What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? (Earth's is 9.8 N/kg.)

options.why: Correct. g ∝ M/R².
g decreases with radius.
g depends on 1/R², not 1/R.
The ratio is inverted.

questions.stem: A 4 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 2t$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 4$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.
Integrate the force over time.
Divide by the mass to get speed.
The force is not constant.

questions.explanation: J = ∫F dt = 16 N·s; v = J/m = 4 m/s.

questions.stem: A 1.1 kg mass oscillates on a spring with $$k = 150$$ N/m. What is the period?

options.why: Include the 2π.
Correct. T = 2π√(m/k).
The ratio is m/k.
That is the frequency.

questions.stem: A 1.5 kg ball on a 1.1 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the top of the circle its speed is 9 m/s. What is the tension in the string there?

options.why: Correct. At the top, T + mg = mv²/r.
Centripetal force uses v².
Check the direction of gravity relative to the center.
Include gravity.

questions.stem: A 8 kg ball moving at +9 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 1 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 1 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: Only equal masses exchange velocities.
Kinetic energy is conserved too.
Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).
That would be a sticking collision.

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = 7 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 16 m/s.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 490 kg load 8 m at constant speed in 30 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: That is the work; divide by time.
Include g.
Correct. P = mgh/t.
P = W/t.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 38 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 7 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.
That is in radians; convert to revolutions.
Recheck the average.
The average angular speed is ω₀/2.

questions.stem: A uniform 7 m beam weighing 200 N rests on supports at both ends. A 500 N load sits 3 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: That is the left support's force.
Include the beam's weight at its center.
The load is not at the center.
Correct. Take torques about the left support.

questions.stem: A boat points straight across a river 200 m wide, moving at 5 m/s relative to the water. The current flows at 3 m/s. How long does the crossing take?

options.why: Correct. The current does not change the time to cross; it only carries the boat downstream.
The perpendicular component alone sets the crossing time.
The current is perpendicular to the heading.
The current is perpendicular to the heading.

questions.stem: Masses of 7 kg and 6 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the tension in the string?

options.why: The heavier mass accelerates down, so T is less than its weight.
Use T = m₂(g + a).
The lighter mass accelerates up, so T exceeds its weight.
Correct. T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).

questions.stem: A constant torque of 17 N·m acts on a wheel ($$I = 1.8$$ kg·m²) initially at rest, through 2 revolutions. What is the wheel's final angular speed?

options.why: ½Iω² = W; solve for ω.
W = ½Iω².
Convert revolutions to radians.
Correct. Work τΔθ (in radians) equals ½Iω².

questions.stem: Satellite B orbits a planet in a circular orbit 3 times the radius of satellite A's circular orbit. What is the ratio of B's orbital speed to A's?

options.why: Farther satellites move more slowly.
Correct. v = √(GM/r), so v ∝ r^(−1/2).

questions.stem: An oscillator's position is $$x(t) = 0.19\cos(9t)$$ m. What is its maximum acceleration?

options.why: Multiply by the amplitude.
Correct. a_max = Aω².
That is v_max.
Differentiate twice: Aω².

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 410$$ N/m is compressed 0.22 m and launches a 1 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: The ½ appears on both sides.
Take the square root.
Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².
Use energy: v = x√(k/m).

questions.stem: A 5 kg block on a horizontal table is connected by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 4 kg block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the table and the block is 0.2. What is the acceleration of the blocks?

options.why: Friction opposes the motion.
Both blocks accelerate; divide by the total mass.
Correct. Net force (m₂g − μm₁g) divided by the total mass.
Include friction on the table block.

questions.stem: An object's acceleration is $$a(t) = 3t$$ m/s². At $$t = 0$$ it has velocity 4 m/s and is at $$x = 0$$. What is its position at $$t = 4$$ s?

options.why: Include the initial velocity.
Correct. Integrate twice, using the initial conditions.
That is the velocity.
Integrating tⁿ divides by n + 1.

questions.stem: A 2 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 6 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: For a disk, I/R² = M/2.
I/R² = M/2.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.
The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 3.92 m/s².

questions.stem: A ball is launched from level ground at 17 m/s at 70° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its horizontal range?

options.why: Use the full time of flight.
That is the maximum range, at 45°.
Range uses sin 2θ.
Correct. Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately.

questions.explanation: v₀x = 5.81 m/s, v₀y = 16 m/s. R = v₀² sin 2θ/g = 19 m.

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 4x^3 - 15x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: dU/dx = 3ax² − b.
Take the square root.
Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 12x² − 15 = 0 gives x = 1.12 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 10 m down a 20° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Friction removes energy.
Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.
Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 4 kg and radius 0.6 m spins at 13 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 1.5 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: Use rotational inertias, not masses.
Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.
The clay's inertia is mR².
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.

questions.stem: A 3000 kg car heading east at 20 m/s collides with a 2000 kg car heading north at 16 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Divide by the total mass.
Weight each velocity by its mass.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.
Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.

questions.stem: An object of mass 0.9 kg falls from rest with a drag force $$F = -bv$$, where $$b = 0.18$$ kg/s. What is its terminal speed?

options.why: Drag here is linear in v.
That is the time constant.
Solve mg = bv for v.
Correct. At terminal speed, mg = bv.

questions.explanation: v_T = mg/b = 49 m/s and τ = m/b = 5 s.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with angular frequency 4 rad/s and amplitude 0.08 m. What is its speed when it is 0.008 m from equilibrium?

options.why: Speed is greatest at equilibrium, not at the ends.
Correct. v = ω√(A² − x²), from conservation of energy.
That is the maximum speed, at x = 0.
Use A² − x² under a square root.

questions.stem: A solid sphere rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 2.9 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: That is only correct for a hoop.
Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ⅖MR².
Some energy goes into rotation.
Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 1 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: The weight acts at L/2.
Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).
τ = MgL/2.
Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 8 kg and radius 0.4 m rotates about an axis perpendicular to it, 1.5 m from its center. What is its rotational inertia?

options.why: The axis is not through the center.
Correct. Parallel-axis theorem: I = ½MR² + Md².
Include the disk's own I about its center.
The parallel-axis term is Md².

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$7 \times 10^{22}$$ kg and radius $$2 \times 10^{7}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.
Take the square root.
Potential energy uses 1/R.
Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.

questions.stem: A rod lies along the x-axis from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 2$$ m and has linear mass density $$\lambda = kx^2$$. Where is its center of mass?

options.why: Integrate x·xⁿ and xⁿ correctly.
Correct. x_cm = ∫xλ dx / ∫λ dx.
The exponents are n + 2 and n + 1.
The rod is not uniform.

questions.stem: A 23 g bullet moving at 300 m/s embeds in a 3.9 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: h = V²/(2g).
Find the block's speed after the collision first.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.
Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.

questions.explanation: V = 1.76 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 0.158 m.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 3 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 1 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.19 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.
Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
